item.passage:
The sign-up sheet for the Fairview Middle School talent show asked for three things: your name, your act, and how long it would take. Owen wrote "Puzzle cube, speed solve" and, after some thought, "under one minute." His best time was thirty-eight seconds. He had set it alone, on a Sunday afternoon at the kitchen table, and he had written the number on the calendar by the phone so that someone else would know it had happened.

Auditions were held in the auditorium on Tuesday after school. Ms. Ferro, who taught music, sat in the sixth row with a clipboard, and beside her sat two eighth graders from the student council. Before Owen, a girl named Leah sang a song from a musical, and two boys juggled tennis balls back and forth across the stage, dropping only two.

Owen walked to the center of the stage, held up the scrambled cube, and said, "Go." He could hear the clicking of the turns come back to him off the far wall. When he set the cube down, finished, he looked at the stopwatch on his wrist: forty-one seconds. It was three seconds slower than his record, which was good enough.

Nobody clapped right away. Ms. Ferro wrote something on her clipboard and asked him to come down and sit in the sixth row for a minute.

"Can I tell you what we saw from here?" she said. "We saw your elbows. We saw your hands moving very fast, and then you put something down. I believe it was impressive. I just couldn't see it."

One of the eighth graders, a tall boy named Rafael, added that from the sixth row the cube had looked about the size of a sugar cube.

Ms. Ferro said Owen could come back on Thursday and try again, if he wanted to.

That night he sat at the kitchen table and solved the cube eleven times while his sister timed him. On the twelfth try he stopped halfway and looked at it. The trouble, he decided, was that a solved cube only looked like something if you had seen it scrambled first. From the sixth row, the beginning and the end were the same small blur.

On Thursday he asked Ms. Ferro to come up onto the stage and scramble the cube herself, as badly as she liked. When she handed it back, he walked slowly along the front edge of the stage, holding it high and turning it so that every row could see the jumble of colors on all six sides. Then he asked the two eighth graders to count the seconds out loud.

He solved it in forty-six seconds, his slowest time in a week, with the counting growing louder the whole way. When he finished, he did not set the cube down. He held it over his head, one solid color facing the seats, and turned it slowly, side by side, the way he had shown them the jumble a minute before.

This time the clapping started before he had finished turning it. That evening Owen looked at the calendar by the phone, where 38 was still written beside the Sunday in March, and below it, in the Thursday square, he wrote 46.

At ten the street goes dark except for this:
a long glass room of white machines,
each with its one round window lit,
and the sign that says OPEN in a red
that hums a little when you stand beneath it.

My mother works till close on Thursdays,
so Thursdays are mine. I carry the bag
three blocks on my shoulder like a sack of flour,
count quarters on the folding table,
and feed them in one by one to a slot that swallows.

Then there is nothing to do but watch.
Our shirts climb the glass and fall,
climb and fall, a slow sleeve waving
as if it knew me. Across the aisle
a man in a work shirt reads a paperback

he holds an inch from his face. Near the door
a woman sleeps upright in a plastic chair,
one hand on a basket of children's clothes,
small socks, a dinosaur on a pajama top.
Her dryer buzzes and she wakes at once,

the way my mother wakes on the couch when I come home,
already reaching. None of us speaks.
We know each other only by our laundry:
his gray towels, her small socks and pajamas,
my mother's blue uniform with the name sewn in,

turning in the windows side by side
like three short films with the sound off.
When mine stops, I lift the warm armful out
and press my face into it for a second,
the way you do when no one you know is watching.

I fold her uniform the way she folds it,
sleeves behind, then thirds, the name on top.
The man looks up and nods at it, or me.
The woman lifts her basket to her hip.
We go out into the dark in three directions,

each of us carrying a warm weight
home against the cold, and the room behind us
keeps its windows lit for whoever comes next,
the drums at rest, waiting to be needed.

a long glass room of white machines,
each with its one round window lit,
and the sign that says OPEN in a red

so Thursdays are mine. I carry the bag

a man in a work shirt reads a paperback

one hand on a basket of children's clothes,
small socks, a dinosaur on a pajama top.

already reaching. None of us speaks.

The building we moved into the spring I was ten had twenty-four apartments and a brass panel of buttons by the front door, one for each, with a name typed on a slip of paper behind a little window. Ours was the last button on the bottom row, 6D, and until summer it had no name at all, only a white slip with a smudge where someone else's had been erased.

On long car trips when I was a child, there came a point, usually somewhere past the second hour, when I had read every sign, counted every cow, and run out of things to look at. I would announce this to the front seat. My father's answer was always the same: "Good. Now something will happen."

For years I took this as a way of telling me to be quiet. I now think he meant it literally. Boredom is an uncomfortable state, and like hunger it is a signal: the mind, having used up what is in front of it, starts looking for something else. What it finds is often more interesting than what it was given. On those trips I invented games, made up the lives of people in passing cars, and once worked out, with my finger on a fogged window, how many fence posts we passed in a minute.

Today that signal rarely gets a chance to sound. A phone in a pocket means that the first flicker of boredom can be answered within seconds, in a waiting room, in a checkout line, at a red light. Each answer is small and harmless. But together they add up to a habit of filling every gap before the mind runs out of things to look at, and so of seldom finding out what it would have done next.

Some researchers have tried to test this. In one well-known kind of study, people are first given a dull task, such as copying numbers out of a phone book, and are then asked to think of as many uses as they can for an ordinary object, like a plastic cup. Those who did the dull task first have often come up with more ideas than those who skipped it. The effects are small, and later studies have been mixed, but they point in the same direction as my father's remark.

None of this means that boredom should be sought out, or that children should be kept from their phones on principle. A long, empty afternoon can be wasted as easily as it can be used. But a few empty minutes are hardly the emergency they have come to feel like.

My own children now ride in the back seat on the same highway, and when they tell me there is nothing to do, I hear myself giving his answer. They find it as unsatisfying as I did. Then, usually within ten minutes, one of them asks me how many fence posts we pass in a minute.

When the railroad reached Kestrel Ford in 1874, it brought a telegraph line with it, strung on poles beside the track, and a small office at the depot to receive it. For its first year the office handled what the railroad needed: train times, freight orders, and now and then a message about a death in some distant family. Most people in town never set foot in it.

The operator was a nineteen-year-old named Ada Brill, who had learned the code from her uncle at a station farther east. Messages reached her as clicks from a brass sounder, and she wrote them down by hand as fast as they came. Between orders, operators along the line often chatted over the wire, and Brill noticed that the stations to the west usually mentioned the weather: rain at Corwin by noon, hail at Tess Crossing, wind out of the northwest.

Storms on the plains around Kestrel Ford generally traveled from west to east. By comparing the chatter with what later arrived outside her own window, Brill worked out that heavy rain reported at Corwin, about sixty miles west, often reached the town two to four hours afterward. item.passage:
Fly over the middle of the Pacific Ocean and you may pass, thousands of kilometers from any continent, a line of green islands strung across the blue like beads on a thread. The Hawaiian Islands are the best known of these chains. Each island is the top of a volcano that began on the sea floor, several kilometers down, and grew upward one eruption at a time until it broke the surface.

Building an island this way takes an enormous amount of rock. Lava that pours out under deep water cools almost at once, forming rounded lumps that geologists call pillow lava, and the volcano grows as a broad underwater mountain. Often only after hundreds of thousands of years of eruptions does its peak reach the waves. Measured from its base on the sea floor, Mauna Kea, on the island of Hawaii, is taller than Mount Everest, though most of that height is underwater.

Why a line of islands rather than a single one? Most geologists explain it with the idea of a hot spot: a place deep beneath the ocean floor where unusually hot rock rises slowly from the mantle and partly melts, feeding volcanoes above it. The hot spot stays in roughly the same place. The Pacific plate, the huge slab of the earth's outer shell that carries the ocean floor, does not; it creeps northwest over the hot spot at several centimeters a year.

So a volcano that forms over the hot spot is slowly carried away from it. Cut off from its supply of melted rock, it stops erupting, and a new volcano begins to grow over the hot spot behind it. Over millions of years the process leaves a chain, much as a sheet of paper pulled slowly over a candle flame would be scorched in a line.

If the hot-spot idea is right, the chain should be youngest at one end and older and older toward the other, and it is. The island of Hawaii, at the southeast end, is roughly a million years old or less and still has active volcanoes. Kauai, farther northwest, is roughly five million years old. Beyond it the islands grow smaller and lower, worn down by rain and waves and sinking as the aging plate beneath them settles. Some end as rings of coral reef around a lagoon where a peak once stood; others slip beneath the surface entirely.

Meanwhile the next island is already on its way. Some thirty-five kilometers off the southeast coast of the island of Hawaii, a young underwater volcano has been active on the sea floor. Its summit is still roughly a kilometer below the waves, and it may need tens of thousands of years to reach the air. By then the plate will have carried the island of Hawaii a little farther to the northwest.
